title: In orbit, a cup with a sharp crease can feed a drink to your lips

cover.alt: A clear plastic cup with orange tape along its edges, held near a small tube aboard the space station.

body: Without gravity, there is no up or down for a drink to settle into, so astronauts usually sip from sealed bags through straws. But liquids in orbit do follow surface tension: where two walls meet at a narrow enough angle, liquid creeps along the joint by itself, with no pump. Astronaut Don Pettit built cups around this, and engineers led by Mark Weislogel later designed one whose bowl narrows into a tapering corner at the lip. Surface tension pulls the drink along the corner towards your mouth, and each sip draws more after it.

slides.alt: A clear plastic cup floats aboard the space station as brown liquid is squirted into it through a tube. The liquid spreads across the cup, then gathers into its narrow corner, where it stays with a smooth curved edge.
slides.caption: Space station, 2012: a drink squirted into Don Pettit's homemade plastic cup is drawn into its narrow corner and stays there instead of floating away.

slides.prompt: Pour a drink into an ordinary cup in orbit and tip it towards your mouth. What happens?
slides.detail: With no gravity, tipping the cup does nothing: the drink stays where surface tension holds it, clinging to the walls, unless a corner draws it along.

slides.question: Besides drinks, what could the same corner trick help move around a spacecraft?
slides.explanation: Corner flows can guide liquids without pumps, from rocket propellants to the water a crew recycles.
